patient.chief_complaint: One year of progressive weakness and numbness in hands and feet, difficulty climbing stairs
patient.history_present_illness: Raymond Kowalski is a 55-year-old retired postal supervisor who presents with a 12-month history of gradually worsening numbness, tingling, and weakness affecting all four extremities. The symptoms began insidiously with bilateral foot numbness described as a 'constant sock feeling,' but over the subsequent months he noticed progressive weakness in his legs, particularly difficulty rising from low chairs, climbing stairs, and walking more than two blocks. His hands became involved about 6 months ago with numbness and grip weakness affecting his ability to open jars and button his shirt. He has fallen twice in the past 4 months. He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction. He notes that his symptoms seem to fluctuate — some weeks feeling slightly better before worsening again — which he initially attributed to activity level. He was evaluated by his primary care physician who noted his HbA1c at 6.1% (prediabetic range) and wondered if this explained his symptoms, but his neurologist is less convinced this fully accounts for the proximal weakness. He has no recent viral illness, vaccination, or new medication prior to symptom onset. He denies alcohol use beyond occasional beer (less than 1 drink per week). Family history includes a paternal aunt with 'some kind of nerve problem' (details unknown). He is otherwise independent in activities of daily living though increasingly struggling.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Glucose 108 mg/dL (H), HbA1c 6.1 % (H), Fasting Glucose 108 mg/dL (H), ESR 32 mm/hr (H), Anti-sulfatide IgM Weakly positive (titer 1:100) (H).

specialized_test.impression: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG. Mixed demyelinating and axonal pattern: distal motor latencies prolonged in upper and lower limbs; F-wave latencies markedly prolonged in bilateral lower extremities; conduction velocities slowed. No unequivocal conduction block or temporal dispersion. Mild acute or chronic reinnervation changes on EMG in proximal lower extremity muscles. Findings indicate a diffuse polyneuropathy with demyelinating features that exceed typical length-dependent axonal patterns

output.interpretation: CSF analysis performed. See findings above.

output.impression: Sural nerve biopsy: segmental demyelination and remyelination with onion bulb formation. Sparse perivascular mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates. No vasculitis. No amyloid deposits. Findings indicate a demyelinating neuropathy with mild inflammatory features; clinical and electrodiagnostic correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), with background prediabetes

differential.key_features: Demyelinating pattern overlaps; would need IgM paraprotein and anti-MAG antibody — SPEP here is negative without M-spike and IgM in normal range.
Important to exclude before IVIG — IgG4 nodopathies are typically IVIG-refractory and respond to rituximab.
HbA1c 6.1% (prediabetes) is too mild to explain proximal weakness, demyelinating velocities, or CSF protein elevation.
Late adult onset, fluctuating course, and absence of pes cavus / hammer toes argue against; CMT1 would show uniformly slow velocities without conduction block but family history is vague.
Mildly elevated ESR but negative ANCA/ANA and a symmetric (not multifocal) pattern; nerve biopsy showed no vasculitis.

optimal_actions.action: Order broad neuropathy labs (CBC, CMP, HbA1c, B12 + MMA, TSH, SPEP/IFE, urinalysis)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify reversible/treatable etiologies (diabetes, B12 deficiency, monoclonal gammopathy, thyroid disease)

optimal_actions.action: Order EMG/NCS to characterize axonal vs demyelinating pattern and distribution
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Length-dependent axonal vs demyelinating vs multifocal pattern; severity and distribution

optimal_actions.action: Search literature for DSP evaluation guidelines and etiology-specific recommendations
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirm AAN 2009 DSP workup, etiology-specific evaluations

optimal_actions.action: Review medications for neurotoxic agents and check interactions for symptomatic therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify potentially neurotoxic drugs (chemotherapy, metronidazole, megadose B6, nitrofurantoin); guide neuropathic-pain pharmacotherapy

optimal_actions.action: Lumbar puncture for CSF when CIDP suspected
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein, normal cell count) supports CIDP

optimal_actions.action: Pre-IVIG safety labs (serum IgA, IgG subclasses, anti-NF155/CNTN1 nodal antibodies)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal IgA (rules out anaphylaxis risk); nodal antibodies negative (anti-NF155+ CIDP responds poorly to IVIG)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy without CNS signs.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: Tier the workup — basic labs first, then targeted electrodiagnostic and tissue studies.
Confirm normal IgA and coagulation before IVIG and LP respectively.

critical_actions: Recognize that demyelinating NCS pattern and proximal weakness are not explained by prediabetes
Obtain CSF to demonstrate albuminocytologic dissociation supporting CIDP
Check serum IgA before any IVIG (anaphylaxis risk with selective IgA deficiency)
Check anti-NF155 / anti-CNTN1 nodal antibodies — IgG4 nodopathies are typically IVIG-refractory
Plan IVIG 2 g/kg induction once safety screen is clear (first-line for CIDP)
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute the picture to prediabetic neuropathy and stop the workup
Do not start IVIG without checking serum IgA
Do not prescribe gabapentin/duloxetine as the only intervention — symptomatic therapy alone misses a treatable demyelinating disease
key_reasoning_points: Demyelinating velocities + prolonged F-waves + proximal EMG changes do not fit a length-dependent diabetic axonal pattern
CSF protein 94 mg/dL with 2 WBC = albuminocytologic dissociation, classic for CIDP
Fluctuating ('relapsing-remitting') course is a defining feature of CIDP
Weakly positive anti-sulfatide IgM (1:100) is a distractor — clinically significant anti-sulfatide neuropathy needs high titers and an IgM paraprotein
IVIG is first-line; pre-treatment safety includes IgA and screening for IgG4 nodopathies

red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on diabetes as cause and stop the workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prediabetes does not produce demyelinating velocities, CSF protein elevation, or proximal weakness; CIDP must be pursued.
Vague family history without pes cavus / hammer toes / childhood onset is non-specific; CMT1 does not fluctuate.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest anti-sulfatide IgM neuropathy as primary diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Clinically meaningful anti-sulfatide neuropathy requires high titers and an IgM paraprotein, neither present here.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required tools, 3 red herrings; classification reflects clinical complexity per PERI-NEURO pack section 6 (M/S/P/R variants).
